'''''Symphytum tuberosum''''', the '''tuberous comfrey''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SYTU|taxon=Symphytum tuberosum|accessdate=7 December 2015}}</ref><ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> is a species of ''[[Symphytum]]'' in the family [[Boraginaceae]].

== Species characteristics ==
[[File:Symphytum tuberosum detail.JPG|left|thumb|190px|Tuberous comfrey flowers.]]
Tuberous comfrey flowers from April to June, however it also reproduces asexually, that is vegetatively, having [[rhizome]]s that allow it to spread out from the original site, colonising and competing as it grows. This process continues into the autumn and the young clonal plants can be seen at this time of year, whilst the parent plants leaves are rotting down. Being very hardy, this plant is well able to survive northern winters.<ref name="The Flora of Skye">[http://www.plant-identification.co.uk/skye/boraginaceae/symphytum-tuberosum.htm The Flora of Skye]</ref> Both the stems and leaves are softly hairy, the leaves have deep veining.<ref name="Medicinal uses">{{cite web |title=Medicinal uses |work=paghat.com |url=http://www.paghat.com/borage.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031003235302/http://www.paghat.com/borage.html |archive-date=October 3, 2003 |url-status=usurped}}</ref>

The flowers themselves are a subtle pale creamy yellow, a significant characteristic for separating its identity from the purple flowered Russian Comfrey. The usual pollinators are the common carder [[bumble bee]], [[honey bee]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.florabeilles.org/serie/symphytum-tuberosum_apis-mellifera|title = Symphytum tuberosum & Apis mellifera|date = 29 January 2018}}</ref> and [[mason bee|red mason bee]]. The stem and leaves are clothed with soft hairs. The stem usually remains unbranched and the leaves are distinctly veined with a clear reduction in size from top to base.

Tuberous comfrey goes dormant in the middle of the summer. Then starts growing again early autumn. Then goes dormant again in the winter, and starts growing late winter or early spring.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Shirley |first=Nancy |title=Botany and History of Comfrey; Garden Uses of Comfrey |date=2022 |publisher=Ingram Publishing |year=2022 |isbn=978-0-9890851-1-3 |location=United States |language=English}}</ref>

== Distribution==
''Symphytum tuberosum'' can be found throughout Europe.<ref>[http://www.ecoflora.co.uk/search_species2.php?plant_no=1480180040 Ecological Flora of the British Isles.]</ref> In Great Britain it is naturally less common in the south,<ref name="Natural England">[http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/o830-tuberouscomfrey.php Natural England] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090531004554/http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/o830-tuberouscomfrey.php |date=2009-05-31 }}</ref> and distribution maps show the species to be common in Scotland and present, but uncommon, throughout much of England and Wales.<ref>[https://data.nbn.org.uk/Taxa/NBNSYS0000003992/Grid_Map NBN Gateway]</ref>

On the [[Isle of Skye]] now it has a well-established and wide distribution thanks to planting,<ref name="The Flora of Skye"/> this has also occurred in Ireland.<ref>[http://www.habitas.org.uk/flora/species.asp?item=3992 Flora of Ireland]</ref> The North American west coast has a number of introduced ''S. tuberosum'' sites.<ref name="Medicinal uses"/>

== Medicinal uses ==
Vernacular common names such as 'knitbone' reveal the healing role that tuberous comfrey and the various hybrid comfreys have played in herbal medicine throughout the ages.<ref name="Natural England"/><ref>[http://193.62.154.38/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/usedata/maxvals=10/firstval=1?SPECIES_XREF=Symphytum+tuberosum Scottish plant uses]</ref> In these traditional cures, the recipes make use of the leaves & roots, the former being used to speed up the healing of minor abrasions through their being applied directly to the damaged skin under a compress.<ref name="Medicinal uses"/>

==Culinary uses==
In spring the fresh young leaves may be used as an herb in cooked recipes, however due to their hairy nature and mildly toxic properties they are not eaten raw. As with dandelion, the root makes a palatable and non-acidic alternative to coffee once prepared, roasted until brown & brittle, and grind it into a powder.
